description: I am Mico, a first-year AI Engineering student at Mapúa University, competing solo. I am building a dashboard that shows where NASA’s combustion data reaches lunar habitat conditions, ranks investigations by relevance, and answers questions with citations. I work in Python, FastAPI, and React, with AI agents helping on extraction and checking.
summary:
On Earth, a flame rises because hot gas floats upward. Aboard a spacecraft nothing floats, and fire behaves differently. NASA has run combustion experiments in microgravity for years, and the results sit in the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository; however, an engineer planning a Moon base cannot easily see which of those experiments match the atmosphere a crew would breathe.

I built Project Counter-Torch, a web dashboard that answers that question. It plots 930 individual tests from four investigations against habitat conditions, and 66 of them fall inside an expected Moon-base atmosphere (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less). It also lists the gaps, such as lunar gravity, where PSI holds no matching data. A fixed formula ranks investigations for a chosen scenario, a compare view shows where related experiments differ, and a question-and-answer view cites its sources and refuses when the records are silent.
details:
Project Counter-Torch has four views. The Coverage view plots 930 tests from NASA's experimental tables (PSI-10, PSI-68, PSI-69 and PSI-159) by oxygen and pressure, draws the expected Moon-base atmosphere on top, and counts the tests inside it: 66, all from the two ACME gaseous-flame experiments. Scrolling reveals the gaps, written by code and not by a model, and a table of all 24 investigation records with a confidence level and a source for every value. The Ranker scores each record for a scenario with a fixed formula (35% conditions, 25% safety function, 20% fuel phase, 20% evidence quality) and explains each score. The Compare view shows only the fields where investigations differ, and an unknown value never counts as a match. The Ask view answers from the loaded records, cites each source, and refuses when too few passages match the question.

The data came from NASA's PSI repository. Oxygen, pressure and airflow ranges for 16 records were computed by script from the experimental tables. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash extracted the other fields, one agent per investigation, and a different model, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B, re-checked all 22 extracted records against their sources. It changed 11 fields across 8 records. I reviewed those changes and ruled on the three records the verifier flagged as disputed. Two records, FM2 and LUCI, remain unverified seed records.

I built the backend with Python and FastAPI, and the web app with React, TypeScript and Vite, using plain SVG and canvas for the charts and background. Claude wrote that code in a Claude Code session under my direction; the agents ran through the Hermes agent framework. The backend has 18 automated tests. No special hardware was needed, and I downloaded no PSI data files, only record details and the small experimental tables.

My intended impact is practical. A researcher or engineer can see which experiments apply to a scenario, how well sourced they are, and which conditions have no data at all, which points the next round of experiments at real gaps.

Three choices shaped the design. First, every value is either sourced or shown as unknown; nothing is guessed. Second, PSI has no true partial-gravity combustion data, so the tool labels partial-gravity scores as bounding estimates from microgravity data and never presents them as measurements. Third, the score measures how relevant and well documented the evidence is; it is not a safety rating. The limits are listed in the repository in docs/data-limitations.md.
dataRefs: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Repository, Combustion Science
